subject: Help me out of nested reactives

messages.author: 6f9739ea511c7a89
messages.subject: Help me out of nested reactives
parts:
Hi all,

I've built a few apps and they work ok'ish, but I just know they are designed poorly.  I end up with nested reactive functions because when I first started playing with shiny, it was the only way my app would work.  Now it's become a habit and I don't know how to get out of it.  I think I need to use observe() or functions, but I don't know how to use them here. Here's the gist of how my server.R usually looks:

[I'm on 3.1 ... trying to kill this bad habit before jumping into 4.0]


shinyServer(function(input, output) {  

  output$wrapper <- reactive(function() {
    main_script()
  })
  
  main_script <- reactive(function() {
    raw_data <- read.csv(input$file$datapath,skip=0,header=TRUE,sep=",")
    user <- input$username

    ##this source'd program takes raw_data and user as inputs
    ##the core output of this source'd program is dataframe cleaned_data
    source("other R program.R",local=TRUE)

    ##now I want to create a bunch of summary views of the cleaned_data dataframe, so I create *nested reactiveTable*, reactiveText, etc
    ##i nest them because that's the only way I've figured out how to give these reactives access to cleaned_data

    output$summary1 <- reactiveTable(function() {
       head(cleaned_data)
    })

    ##and the madness continues ... I nest a reactivePlot within this reactiveTable because I want the plot to have access to the table 
    output$summary2 <- reactiveTable(function() {
       t <- sqldf("SELECT a, SUM(clicks)  FROM cleaned_data GROUP BY 1)

       #i nest the reactive plot within here because I want access to t
       output$graph <- reactivePlot(function() {
           blahblahblah
        })
        t
     })
})

messages.author: 55771919c42cb6a1
messages.subject: Re: Help me out of nested reactives
parts:
The key is that if you use a reactive expression (formerly known as "reactive function"), its value gets cached, and it only re-executes when it depends on variables that have changed. So you could do something like this to use cleaned data in two output objects, and it'll only execute the clean_data() reactive expression once:

shinyServer(function(input, output) {  
  clean_data <- reactive ({
    # Do something based on input$foo, and return a data frame
  })

  output$mytable <- renderTable({
    clean_data()
  })

  output$myplot <- renderPlot({
    data <- clean_data()
    plot(data$x, data$y)
  })
})


Note that this code is written for Shiny 0.4.0; if you want it to work with previous versions:
* Replace reactive({ }) with reactive(function() { })
* Replace renderTable({ }) with reactiveTable(function() { })
* Replace renderPlot({ }) with reactivePlot(function() { })


There are some new parts of the tutorial that explain how this works:
http://rstudio.github.com/shiny/tutorial/#reactivity-overview


-Winston

messages.author: ca443e6eaa0e78ed
messages.subject: Re: Help me out of nested reactives
parts:
Are you sure we didn't recommend you use reactiveValue and observers to implement insulated reactives? I couldn't find the thread where we talked about this so for the benefit of everyone let me expound on laziness and insulation.

We use the term "laziness" to mean: when a reactive expression (what we used to call reactive functions, before Shiny 0.4.0) notices that one of the reactive values/expressions that it depends on has changed, it does nothing other than notifying its dependent reactive expressions/observers that it has been invalidated. It doesn't re-execute itself or schedule itself to be re-executed.

We use the term "insulation" to mean that if one of the reactive values/expressions in your graph of dependencies (things that YOU depend on, not the other way around) changes, but before the chain reaches you the value is noticed to be the same as it was before, then you don't get invalidated. Here's a concrete example.

approxCount <- reactive({
  input$count - (input$count %% 10)
})

observe({
  cat(paste("Count has reached:", approxCount()))
})

The approxCount reactive expression rounds input$count to the nearest 10. So if input$count changes from 1 to 2, approxCount's value is recalculated and the result is 0 in both cases.

If reactive expressions don't provide insulation, then as input$count goes from 0, 1, 2... 10 you will see the output printed 11 times, with many duplicates. If reactive expressions provide insulation, then you will only see the output printed twice, with no duplicates.

Before Shiny 0.4.0, reactive functions were not lazy but provided insulation.
With Shiny 0.4.0, reactive expressions (née functions) are lazy but do not provide insulation.

It is not possible to have a single reactive construct that provides both laziness and insulation--these two goals are inherently exclusive. In real-world apps it appeared to us that laziness mattered way more often than insulation did. (For example, if you want tabs that are not showing to not cost you any recalculation time, you need laziness.)

It would be possible to introduce a different construct (insulatingReactive(), or maybe reactive({..}, lazy=FALSE)) that provides insulation, but we don't have one today. However you can combine reactiveValue and observers to achieve insulation:

values <- reactiveValues(approxCount=NULL)

observe({
  values$approxCount <- input$count - (input$count %% 10)
})

observe({
  cat(paste("Count has reached:", values$approxCount))
})

I'm not sure how you would combine reactiveValue and observers to achieve laziness though, or why you'd need to do anything special to get laziness in Shiny 0.4.0.
